name: Head & Shoulders

lead:
Head & Shoulders is a widely sold anti-dandruff shampoo made by Procter & Gamble. Dandruff shows as white or grey flakes on the scalp, hair and clothing, so treating it changes how a person's hair and grooming look.
The brand's antifungal active is zinc pyrithione or piroctone olamine, with selenium disulfide in some clinical-strength versions. Dermatology sources list those ingredients among those with evidence of effectiveness against dandruff, which is linked to the yeast Malassezia.

paras: It is used as a regular shampoo, lathered on the scalp as a part of a normal wash routine. Variants include shampoo-and-conditioner products and stronger clinical formulas.

Dandruff shampoos are generally well tolerated, though scalp irritation is possible with any active. Anyone with persistent flaking, hair loss or inflamed skin is typically directed to a dermatologist.

chain: Antifungal shampoo ingredients act on scalp Malassezia
angle.text: Head & Shoulders addresses visible flaking: the antifungal active reduces the yeast linked to dandruff, so fewer white flakes show in the hair and on clothing. The result is a tidier, cleaner-looking head of hair while the shampoo is used.

lead: Head & Shoulders is an American anti-dandruff shampoo brand owned by Procter & Gamble (P&G), previously owned by Richardson Vicks. It launched in the United States in 1961 after roughly a decade of P&G research into dandruff, and its trademark was registered in 1962 [1]. By its 50th anniversary in 2011 it was reported as the world's largest-selling shampoo brand, at roughly 29 million units a year [1].

People use it to remove the visible flakes of dandruff, which affects about half of adults and is more common in men, usually starting at puberty [2]. White flakes in the hair and on dark clothing are a conspicuous grooming issue, so a shampoo that controls them supports a cleaner overall look: tidier hair, a clearer scalp and clean-looking shoulders. The brand's advertising has long made exactly that link between flakes and first impressions [1].

The brand's main antifungal active is zinc pyrithione or piroctone olamine, and some clinical-strength versions also contain selenium disulfide [1]. Dermatology references list these among antifungal shampoo ingredients with evidence of effectiveness against dandruff, which is associated with the scalp yeast Malassezia [2][3]. Controlled trials of zinc pyrithione shampoos, including a split-scalp study from the 1980s and a multicentre comparison with ketoconazole, are described below [4].

paras: Head & Shoulders is sold as a shampoo and as combined shampoo-and-conditioner products, with additional versions marketed for specific hair or scalp needs. Its main antifungal ingredient is piroctone olamine or zinc pyrithione, and clinical-strength versions add selenium disulfide [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, lists product lines including Classic Clean, Dry Scalp Care, 2-in-1 shampoo-conditioners, Classics for Men, Supreme for colour-treated hair, a Clinical Strength range, and a nine-ingredient BARE line launched in 2023 [5].

The same account says most versions use 1% zinc pyrithione, some European and UK lines use piroctone olamine instead, and Clinical Strength uses 1% selenium sulfide for severe cases [5]. Formulas differ by market and over time.

sections.h: Dandruff and how the shampoo works
paras: Dandruff is a common scalp condition of itching and flaking. Its cause is not fully settled, but genetic and environmental factors are thought to play a part, and it is not caused by poor hygiene [2]. Flakes are thought to form when skin cells mature and shed in about 2 to 7 days instead of roughly a month [2].

Dandruff is linked to the fungus Malassezia, particularly M. globosa, which breaks down scalp oil with lipase enzymes into oleic acid that can irritate skin and trigger inflammation. People with dandruff have roughly 1.5 to 2 times the normal amount of Malassezia [2]. A 2007 genome study of M. globosa found eight lipases and three phospholipases among its genes, and its authors suggested these proteins as possible targets for dandruff treatments [3]. Seborrhoeic dermatitis, the more inflammatory form, is thought to involve a local inflammatory response to Malassezia in sebum-rich skin, together with skin-barrier and immune factors [6].

Zinc pyrithione, selenium disulfide, piroctone olamine and ketoconazole are antifungal shampoo ingredients listed with evidence of effectiveness, and ketoconazole appears to last longer [2]. Zinc pyrithione is thought to interfere with fungal membrane transport, and a 2011 study proposed a mechanism involving copper and iron-sulphur proteins [7]. Salicylic acid and coal tar are other recognised anti-dandruff actives that work by shedding dead skin cells [2].

P&G began dandruff research around 1950, and after about ten years its scientists developed a zinc pyrithione shampoo [1]. A patent on zinc pyrithione anti-dandruff shampoos, assigned jointly to P&G and the R. T. Vanderbilt Company, was issued in 1966 and traces to applications from 1958 [1]. The product was introduced in the United States on 1 January 1961, and the trademark was registered in 1962 [1].

Grokipedia attributes the project to chemist John Parran Jr., recruited in 1949 for a secretly coded effort, and says more than 1,000 compounds were screened; it also gives a 1973 UK launch, a switch from cream to liquid in 1975, and an Indian launch in 1997. These details come from an AI-generated page and are not independently confirmed here [5].

In 1988 the brand became the first P&G brand launched in mainland China [1]. A 1982 publication noted heavy advertising spend and said no other brand matched its sales despite being a medicated shampoo [1]. A 1966 item titled 'Head and Shoulders' in The Medical Letter on Drugs and Therapeutics shows the product was also being assessed in the medical press in its early years [8].

The brand's advertising has long tied dandruff to appearance and social embarrassment. Its best-known tagline is 'You Never Get a Second Chance to Make a First Impression,' and critics have described the approach as anxiety marketing built on fear of social consequences [1]. Later advertising has tried to move the brand away from a medicinal image and to reduce the stigma of using an anti-dandruff shampoo [1].

Grokipedia lists a 'Don't' campaign beginning in 1990, athlete partnerships including Troy Polamalu, Patrick Mahomes and Aidan Hutchinson, sponsorship of England national football teams, a #FreeTheShoulders anti-bullying initiative with The Diana Award from 2021 to 2023, and regional campaigns in Vietnam [5]. In 2006, the UK Advertising Standards Authority upheld complaints about two advertisements over 'up to 100%' claims, according to the same page [5].

The shampoo itself is rarely discussed as a looksmaxxing topic. Forum conversation that mentions 'shoulders' is almost entirely about shoulder width, posture and lateral-raise training for a broader frame, which is a separate subject from the shampoo. Dandruff control appears in general grooming advice as part of keeping hair and skin presentable, and the shampoo is one of several anti-dandruff options on the market.

Published trials mostly test the active ingredients rather than the branded product. In a 1985 British Journal of Dermatology study, 32 people with dandruff washed one half of the scalp with a 1% zinc pyrithione shampoo and the other half with the same shampoo without it. Dandruff declined progressively on the treated side, the difference was significant after three or more washes, and treated areas had fewer microorganisms on staining [4].

A 2002 open, multicentre randomised trial in 331 participants with severe dandruff or seborrheic dermatitis compared 2% ketoconazole with 1% zinc pyrithione shampoos. Both improved symptoms, ketoconazole was significantly better at week 4 and had a lower recurrence rate, and both were well tolerated [4]. A 2011 trial comparing a piroctone olamine and climbazole shampoo with a 1% zinc pyrithione shampoo in moderate to severe dandruff found comparable antifungal activity and equal reduction of dandruff [4].

A 2012 transcriptional study of scalp biopsies found increased inflammatory gene activity and reduced lipid-metabolism gene activity in dandruff-affected skin, and a zinc pyrithione shampoo shifted the affected profile toward that of normal scalp [4].

Dandruff shampoos are generally well tolerated, with minimal side effects reported in comparative trials [4]. Zinc pyrithione is classified in the EU as a category 1B reproductive toxicant, and its use in EU cosmetic products has been prohibited since December 2021 under Regulation (EU) 2021/1902; the US permits up to 2% in rinse-off products [7][6]. Because of this, UK and European Head & Shoulders ranges use piroctone olamine in some lines, according to Grokipedia [5].

Grokipedia also records user reports of breakouts from shampoo residue, salon concerns about build-up on tools, packaging and animal-testing questions, and states that claims the product causes hair loss are unsupported [5]. P&G's 2021 benzene recall concerned aerosol dry shampoo and conditioner sprays from other brands, not Head & Shoulders liquid shampoo.

Alternatives and complements include ketoconazole shampoo, selenium sulfide, salicylic acid and coal tar products, and gentle cleansers for dry scalp, which is a different condition from dandruff [2][6]. Persistent flaking, redness or hair shedding is generally referred to a dermatologist [6].
